title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E555 Euler builds an infinite Lagrange-type interpolation series. It passes a curve through the points x=(n+i)θ, y=sin(n+i)θ. In §31-32, with θ=π, this gives the partial-fraction series whose sum is (π/2ω)tan ωπ, and he concludes Δ=(1+2ω)π/cos ωπ. §33, which starts on the previous page and ends here, raises the uniqueness problem. Infinitely many curves pass through the same nodes. So the general solution is y=Θ+f(Ω), where:
- Θ is the interpolant he found;
- Ω=ω(n²−ω²)·Π_{k≥1}((n+k)²−ω²)/(k(2n+k)) = 2ω(n+ω)/Δ is the canonical entire function vanishing at all the nodes ω=0, ±(n+k);
- f is any function with f(0)=0.
Whether Θ equals sin ωθ may depend on n and θ.

Scholion 2 (§34) specialises to θ=π, n=1/2. Then Θ=π(1+2ω)tan ωπ/Δ.
- Admissible added terms vanish at ω=0, ±1/2, ±3/2, ...: sin 2iωπ, ω cos(2i−1)ωπ and combinations of them. All of these do vanish there (checked).
- Writing sin ωπ=Θ+Φ gives Δ=π(1+2ω)tan ωπ/(sin ωπ−Φ), with Δ also given as a Beta integral.
- At ω=0 the integral gives Δ=π. Hence Φ must be o(ω), i.e. Φ contains ω^λ with λ>1; otherwise Δ(0)≠π.
- From this he declares the conclusions of the earlier problem valid.

In modern terms, this is the uniqueness question for interpolating an entire function on a lattice, which is borderline here. sin πω and the node-vanishing function ω cos πω both have exponential type π (Carlson-type situation).

In fact Φ≡0 can be proved exactly with Euler's own tools. For n=1/2, Wallis' product plus the cosine product give Ω=ω cos(πω)/π. Hence Δ=π(1+2ω)/cos πω and Θ=sin ωπ identically.

Problem 4 (§35) begins a new interpolation problem with nodes on two interleaved shifted lattices x=(k±n)θ. The ansatz is y∝𝔄p/n−𝔅q/(1−n)+..., with coefficients given by infinite products. The next page evaluates these by Beta integrals.
errors: The Beta-integral form of Δ as printed/transcribed, Δ=2∫z^{1/2−ω}(1−z)^{−1/2−ω}dz, does not equal π(1+2ω)/cos ωπ. It equals 2^{2ω}√π Γ(1/2−ω)/Γ(1−ω); for example, at ω=1/4 it gives ≈7.416 versus ≈6.664. The correct form is Δ=2∫z^{1/2+ω}(1−z)^{−1/2−ω}dz = 2B(3/2+ω,1/2−ω) = (1+2ω)Γ(1/2+ω)Γ(1/2−ω). Both forms agree at ω=0, so Euler's ω=0 check cannot detect the sign slip. It is unclear whether the slip is a misprint or Euler's own.
The argument that Φ has a factor ω^λ with λ>1 only shows Φ=o(ω) near 0; it does not prove Φ≡0. The conclusion is nevertheless true here, because Ω can be evaluated in closed form.

ideas.what: General interpolating curve = particular interpolant + arbitrary function of a node-vanishing entire function (the canonical product Ω)
ideas.modern_name: Non-uniqueness of interpolation; adding multiples of a function vanishing on the nodes (Weierstrass-product kernel)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (the non-uniqueness remark for factorial interpolation); later Weierstrass, Carlson (1914) for uniqueness criteria
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opera omnia I.15); similar remarks occur in Euler's Gamma-interpolation work, with exact locations unsure

ideas.what: Explicit catalogue of functions vanishing at 0, ±1/2, ±3/2, ...: sin 2iωπ and ω cos(2i−1)ωπ
ideas.modern_name: Entire functions vanishing on a lattice; periodic perturbations

ideas.what: Using the value at ω=0 (Δ=π from the Beta integral) to force the perturbation Φ to vanish to order >1
ideas.modern_name: Heuristic uniqueness test; distant precursor of growth or local-condition uniqueness theorems (Carlson, Bohr–Mollerup style)

ideas.what: Interpolation series with nodes on two interleaved lattices (k±n)θ, coefficients as infinite products evaluated by Beta integrals
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange/cardinal-type interpolation series on nonuniform (union of shifted lattices) nodes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cardinal series: Whittaker 1915; nonuniform sampling: later 20th c.

missed.claim: Euler's discussion is a clear early instance of the uniqueness problem for interpolating entire functions of exponential type on a lattice. It includes the borderline case where sin πω and the node function ω cos πω have the same type π, and the test 'Φ must vanish to order >1 at 0' to pin down the interpolant. This anticipates the issues later settled by Carlson's theorem and by sampling theory. Links between E555 and the sampling/cardinal-series literature may exist (e.g. in Butzer's historical work) but I am unsure.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority for uniqueness questions in sampling and interpolation theory.

deep.surprise_reason: The interpolation-series ideas are in a published paper (E555, Opera omnia I.15). The explicit treatment of non-uniqueness by adding node-vanishing functions, and the borderline exponential-type situation, is a nice anticipation of Carlson and sampling theory. However, it is not hidden, and the Beta-exponent sign slip is minor.
transcription_corrections: First line: the factors should read ω(nn−ωω)·((n+1)²−ω²)/(1(2n+1))·((n+2)²−ω²)/(2(2n+2))·etc., not 2(2n+1)·3(2n+3). This matches k(k+1) denominators for n=1/2 and the Wallis evaluation Ω=ω cos πω/π.
In §34 the integral exponent appears as x^{1/2−ω}. For consistency with Δ=π(1+2ω)/cos ωπ it should be x^{1/2+ω}; check the original print.
The argument of f in §34 should be Ω=ω(1+2ω)/Δ for n=1/2; the transcribed '/(2Δ)' is doubtful, though f is arbitrary anyway.
The left side of the Problem 4 ansatz ('y/ω') is uncertain in the image.
